skeleton:
Feseekh Rolls

Egyptian · Hard · Serves 4, cautiously

Jump to Recipe Method Troubleshooting Storage
Feseekh — salt-cured, air-dried mullet, Egypt's Sham El-Nessim spring festival fish — is one of the world's great fermented foods and one of its most polarizing: gray, intense, ammoniated, ancient. This site records it honestly and serves it in its modern softened format: the feseekh flaked small, mellowed with boiled potato and olive oil into a spread for rolls, with the sharp garnishes its power demands. The salt-curing craft (#17's own logic, taken to fermentation's far shore) is not this recipe's work — the fish is bought cured — and the safety law below is the recipe's first paragraph disguised as a paragraph. **The safety law, stated plainly:** feseekh is a fermented fish, and its preparation has hospitalized the careless. Buy it only from a licensed Egyptian or specialized producer, cured and packed properly; never attempt home-curing (the #92 preserved-lemon record is the safe face of this preserving family); refrigerate it always; and discard any batch that smells of anything beyond its own intense register. This recipe is assembly, and the assembly's care is the dish.

Quantities live in the recipe card.

  • the fish carries it)
- **Bone the fish twice — once by eye, once by fingertip.** Feseekh's fine bones hide in the flakes; a smear spread on a plate and run over with the fingertips finds what the eye misses. This is the one craft the home cook owes the dish, beyond the sourcing. - **The bridge:** feseekh itself does not bridge — it is its own argument. If the fermented fish is past your line, this format (the spread, the sharp garnishes, the cool salad in a roll) belongs to smoked mackerel or salt cod by the same assembly, and you will have learned the sandwich, which was the point.

Feseekh Rolls

Prep: 15 minutes · Cook: No cook · Total: About 30 minutes, assembly only · Serves 4, cautiously

Ingredients

Ingredients

  • 250 g properly cured feseekh fillet (from a licensed producer), skinned, boned with absolute care, flaked very fine
  • 2 medium boiled potatoes (about 300 g, or roughly 150 g each), mashed smooth — the mellowing body
  • 3–4 tbsp good olive oil (about 50 g); the juice of ½ a lemon
  • A pinch of cumin; black pepper (no salt — the fish carries it)
  • 4 soft rolls (about 250 g), split; lettuce leaves (about 50 g), sliced tomato (about 100 g), and very thin red onion (about 30 g)
  • The sharp garnish plate: more lemon, finely chopped green chili, and a dish of #99 zhug or #91 harissa thinned with oil

Instructions

  1. **Make the spread (10 minutes).** Flake the feseekh very fine, then work it with the warm mashed potato and olive oil to a soft, spoonable paste — the proportions run by taste: more potato for gentleness, more fish for the festival. Lemon and cumin at the end, folded. Checkpoint — the spread should be intensely savory, saline, and unmistakably itself — the potato rounds without diluting, the oil carrying, the lemon lifting just enough. Taste and adjust toward your household's courage level, knowing the festival version runs fierce.
  2. **Build the rolls (5 minutes).** The split rolls lined with lettuce (the barrier the spread needs), a generous spoon of the feseekh spread, tomato and the paper-thin onion over, lemon and chili at the diner's hand. Checkpoint — eating test: the roll's soft chew, the spread's concentrated fermented depth — sea, salt, and the ammoniated edge that Egypt's spring festival celebrates — the onion's bite and lemon's cut running against it, the tomato cooling. It should be fierce and refreshing at once, and the sharp garnishes are the architecture that makes the fiercest preserved fish eatable in the noon sun of a national holiday.

Troubleshooting

SymptomCauseFix
Off, wrong smell beyond feseekh's ownBad batchDiscard entirely \u2014 the law has no exceptions
Spread overwhelmingly fierceFish-to-potato ratio highMore potato, more lemon; adjust by feel
Bones in the spreadUnder-checked flakesThe plate-and-fingertip pass, always

Storage, Make-Ahead & Variations

- The spread keeps 1 day refrigerated, tightly covered (no longer — its intensity grows); the rolls are assembled to the minute. The cured fish keeps per the producer's instruction, refrigerated. - Variations: the festival plate (feseekh whole beside the spring onions and lettuce leaves, the sandwich unbuilt); the salt-cod or smoked-mackerel bridge version. The #92 preserved lemons are this fermenting family's daily face on this site.
